title: Ways to Secure a Load
whatItIs: Lashings, chains, headboards, chocks and friction matting work together. Each has its own rules, from attachment points to headboard gaps.

keyFacts.text: You MUST NOT attach more than one lashing to an anchorage point, or thread one through and hook it back on itself.
Sheeting or rope hooks MUST NOT be used as anchors for straps or chains.
Straps and chains MUST NOT be combined in the same lashing: they stretch differently.
If the headboard is part of the system, the load MUST be against it or within 30 cm wherever possible.

items.title: Chains
items.text: Usually stronger than straps. Heavy plant by direct lashing: at least 4 chains.

items.title: Headboards
items.text: Load against it or within 30 cm. If not, block it or add lashings.

items.title: Friction matting
items.text: Never use it on its own. Should have a coefficient of friction of at least 0.6.

items.title: Chocks and cradles
items.text: Barriers to movement. Used with lashings, but fewer may be needed.

items.title: Strap label
items.text: Use LC for direct lashing and STF for frictional lashing.

items.title: Ropes
items.text: Not for securing a load for the journey.

a.label: Frictional (tie-down) lashing
points: Presses the load down onto the load bed

b.label: Direct lashing
points: One end on the load, the other on the vehicle

onTheTest.question: Your frictional lashings over a low load are at less than 30° to the load bed. What does the guidance say?
options: It's fine if the straps are new
onTheTest.why: Frictional lashing works best close to vertical. Under 30° it won't be effective: raise the load (for example, with empty pallets) or use another method.

onTheTest.question: Which of these is a suitable point to attach a lashing strap to?
options: A sheeting hook on the side rave
A dedicated anchorage point in good condition
A chain already securing the load
onTheTest.why: Attach to the chassis, side raves or dedicated anchorage points. Sheeting and rope hooks aren't designed for load securing.

traps: Strap involved in a load shift? Don't reuse it if worn or damaged, even slightly.
Never tie a knot in any part of a strap that's under tension.
BS 5759 straps are withdrawn: replace them with straps made to BS EN 12195-2.
